title: "The Sovereign Citizen" & "Freeman-On-The-Land" Argument
summary: A lawyer warns that renouncing citizenship as a sovereign individual escapes no debts, taxes or charges and invites sanctions and contempt.

assertions.quote: Courts typically find this being frivolous.

verdicts.note: The Seventh Circuit lists repeated rejections of sovereign, immunity and flesh-and-blood theories ('no conceivable validity in American law', frivolous) and says they should be rejected summarily; one circuit's view, but stated as settled.
Ohio appeals court: this court and many others have repeatedly rejected these right-to-travel and sovereign claims, which 'continue to make their way to court and fail'.
Queensland Court of Appeal dismissed a 'citizen sovereign' unlicensed-driving appeal as 'obvious nonsense' and an abuse of process.

Court-staff author reports there is 'no legal substance' to these concepts, appeals are disposed of perfunctorily and all 51 OPCA leave applications to the Supreme Court of Canada were denied; the one exception, the 1968 Credit River case, was declared a nullity.

In tax cases, claims of being a sovereign or solely a state citizen are 'uniformly rejected' and called frivolous and clearly baseless (Fed. Cl. Wells, 5th Cir. Bowden); evidence is limited to tax litigation.
Across over 700 Canadian reported judgments, the author says courts consistently rejected OPCA ideas; the few acquittals rested on Crown evidentiary gaps and were later disapproved.
The review of 200+ cases says no court accepts pseudolegal arguments or relieves a claimant of their obligations; they are often called 'gibberish' or 'obvious nonsense'.
In 1089 Canadian OPCA decisions the litigation was invariably unsuccessful, and all 51 OPCA-linked Supreme Court leave applications were refused; no court anywhere has endorsed the memeplex.
Review notes high-profile defendants' sovereign-citizen strategies have all failed and were deemed frivolous; illustrative, not a systematic count.

assertions.quote: It will be met with sanctions. It'll be met with um allegations of frivolous conduct.

verdicts.note: Author (court litigant-management counsel) says OPCA litigation is often self-destructive, endorsing the quip that it turns a $50 traffic ticket into jail as 'the truth'.

Raising frivolous positions adds penalties of up to $25,000 in Tax Court (IRC 6673), appellate Rule 38 sanctions, and possible fraud penalties on top of the tax owed; the document does not directly compare outcomes with normal arguments.
The author says OPCA ideas damage their adherents, who see others fail and face sanction, but gives no comparison with arguing normally.
The authors say pseudolegal arguments never work and turn simple legal issues into costlier, harmful ones; litigants waste time and money and give up proper representation.

assertions.quote: You can't just opt out of laws in the country because suddenly you're, you know, you proclaim yourself to not be a citizen.

verdicts.note: By statute a 'national of the United States' includes every citizen; non-citizen national status comes from birth in outlying possessions such as American Samoa, not from a declaration, and no provision exempts nationals from law.

Circuits rejected claims that being a citizen of a state or 'state republic' rather than the US puts one beyond federal court jurisdiction (2d Cir. Drachenberg, 7th Cir. Hilgeford); federal tax context only, so state jurisdiction is not covered.

assertions.quote: they go into the prison system, they read a couple of books, somebody gives them this great idea that they should revoke their citizenship

verdicts.note: The court notes a nationwide increase since 2004 in unsubstantiated liens filed by prison inmates against officials. That shows use among inmates, not how the ideas spread.
A bank-robbery accused got his Coronation Oath theory from a samizdat circulating in Alberta remand centres; one documented example.
FBI says imprisoned sovereign citizens recruit and train other inmates in the ideology and fraud methods.
Review says the message spreads through jails and prisons via mailers and word of mouth, including a $4000 'bond process' scheme sold to prisoners.

assertions.quote: That just proves that you signed it. That's what a notary does.

verdicts.note: Notarization authenticates the signer's identity and signature; it does not validate the document's contents.

The court says a plaintiff cannot create a legal obligation 'simply by stating in a document that the obligation exists and then having the document notarized'. This supports the claim that notarizing adds no legal force.
A Quebec notary who 'acted as a judge' to end a debt collection produced a document the court called frivolous; notarisation added no legal force.
